Session 1 Facilitator Rehearsal Run Sheet

Re-own the product decision

Version: 2026-08-22 Format: 135-minute live cohort session Cohort: up to 10 PMs with approximately 2-6 years of experience Deck: 19-page HTML/PDF facilitator deck Preparation: learners complete the integrated Session 1 pre-read before the live session

This is a rehearsal document, not a teleprompter. The script is intentionally fuller than anything that should be spoken word for word. Rehearse the logic, examples, questions, and transitions; then teach in your own voice.

The facilitator's job

By the end of the session, learners should be able to make one product decision inspectable because they can separate:

  1. the decision from the activity;
  2. the evidence from their interpretation;
  3. the user request from the audience-problem-value hypothesis; and
  4. a responsible next move from a premature product commitment.

The governing message is:

PM core skill is not producing more product work. It is taking accountable positions on consequential choices while making the evidence boundary, uncertainty, and revision conditions visible.

Keep the session decision-led. Do not reteach the pre-read paragraph by paragraph. The live value is in the tensions: speed versus rigor, evidence versus judgment, position versus certainty, and problem definition versus feature commitment.

What changed after the facilitator read-through

  • The decision-rigor exhibit now uses qualitative signals rather than bars that could be mistaken for a scoring model.
  • The three-input exhibit now describes each input's job and limitation rather than implying numerical weights.
  • The Unit 1 reversibility example now stays on the onboarding decision instead of jumping prematurely to the Unit 3 summary request.
  • The Noted case is visibly labeled as a real product context with constructed evidence. Constructed case material is valid for practice, not proof of market demand.WN-01
  • The option comparison now uses qualitative language rather than pseudo-precise bar lengths.
  • This run sheet adds model debriefs, misconception recoveries, transitions, and source pins that should stay off the learner-facing slides.

Before learners arrive

  • Open the HTML deck and verify arrow-key navigation and fullscreen mode.
  • Keep a visible six-minute timer ready for slides 8, 13, and 17.
  • Prepare one capture surface with four headings: decision, reason against, boundary, and revision trigger.
  • Ask learners to keep their answer private until the six minutes end. This prevents the first confident answer from anchoring the room.
  • Select responses yourself. There is no peer critique or required peer discussion. Invite two or three learners to state their decision directly to you; you compare the reasoning.
  • Do not reveal a model answer before the decision time. A polished answer copied from the facilitator produces no evidence of judgment.
  • Treat every Noted number, interview, persona, and stakeholder statement as constructed course evidence unless the repository provenance says otherwise. The product, code, and repository workflow are real; most research and company context are constructed.WN-01

Facilitation stance

Use four moves throughout:

  1. Ask for the decision. If a learner gives a topic, activity, or deliverable, ask: "What choice could go differently?"
  2. Ask for the boundary. If a learner makes a broad claim, ask: "For whom, over what period, and supported by which evidence?"
  3. Ask for the strongest reason against the view. Do not accept a token caveat.
  4. Ask what would change the recommendation. A view that cannot name a revision condition is a position being defended, not a belief being managed.

Useful recovery phrases:

  • "That is an activity. What decision is the activity meant to change?"
  • "You may be right. Which observation supports that, and which part is your interpretation?"
  • "What population can this evidence actually speak for?"
  • "If the request disappeared tomorrow, what underlying objective would still remain?"
  • "What would have to be true for the no-build option to be better?"
  • "You said it depends. Name the dependency and make the call under your current assumption."

Avoid these phrases:

  • "The data proves..."
  • "The customer validated..."
  • "The score says..."
  • "The right answer is..."
  • "We just need more data."
  • "This is reversible" without naming exposure, rollback, stop conditions, and residual cost.

Slide-by-slide rehearsal script

Slide 1 - Re-own the product decision

Time: 4 minutes Job: Reframe "core PM" as accountable judgment before artifacts and methods.

Rehearse

"This course begins before the roadmap, before the PRD, before the prototype, and before the research plan. Those are all useful. But each is downstream of a product decision. If the decision is weak or invisible, faster execution only gets us to the wrong place with more confidence."
"For experienced PMs, the risk is not that you cannot run the process. You probably can. The risk is that the process slowly becomes the job: intake, alignment, backlog, meetings, and artifacts. Session 1 is about re-owning the judgment underneath that machinery."
"Today we will make three moves. We will choose which decision deserves PM attention. We will form a current product view without pretending certainty. Then we will earn a problem definition without converting it immediately into a feature."

Emphasize that leverage means changing the impact-to-effort relationship, not increasing visible activity. Decision and meeting volume can crowd out the work that needs PM judgment.S1-SN-01S1-SN-02

Ask

"Think of your last full week. How much of it was spent making a consequential product judgment, rather than moving product work through the system?"

Do not collect answers yet. Let the question create the tension.

Transition

"The three moves are not three templates. They are one chain. Let me show you the record we are building."

Slide 2 - One inspectable decision record

Time: 6 minutes Job: Establish the cumulative logic and the teach-decide-debrief contract.

Rehearse

"The first move is a decision boundary: what choice, owned by whom, affecting which population, over what horizon, with what material consequence?"
"The second move is a current product view: what do we observe, what do we infer, what prior experience are we using, how strongly do we hold the position, and what would change it?"
"The third move is a linked hypothesis: which audience, which problem, what promised value relative to the current alternative, and which claim is weak enough to determine the next evidence work?"
"At the end you will not have three completed forms. You will have one record another PM can inspect. They should be able to disagree with you without first reconstructing how you got there."

Explain the rhythm:

"For each unit I will teach the judgment, then you will make an individual call on the same Noted case. I will ask for two or three answers. We are not voting and we are not searching for a hidden answer key. We are comparing the quality and boundaries of the reasoning."

Listen for

Learners may assume they will be assessed on completeness. Correct early:

"A complete-looking record can still contain weak judgment. An incomplete record that names the decisive unknown can be much stronger."

Transition

"So let us start without a framework. Here is Monday morning at Noted."

Slide 3 - Four competing signals

Time: 6 minutes Job: Create genuine competition for attention before explaining how to choose.

Rehearse

"Noted is a real note-taking and AI workspace product. For this exercise, the numbers and stakeholder signals on this slide are constructed. That makes them legitimate inputs for practice, but not real market evidence. Keep that distinction alive; provenance is part of product judgment."WN-01

Walk through the four signals without interpreting them:

  • New-user activation is down 11 percent across six weeks.
  • Three enterprise customers have requested automated summaries.
  • Large-workspace latency has worsened.
  • A platform dependency reaches end of support in ten weeks.

Then say:

"Notice what your mind just did. Some of you prioritized the red number. Some prioritized the customers. Some saw reliability or platform risk as obviously more important. That first reaction is useful as a prior, but it is not yet a decision."
"Also notice that these may not all need PM attention. A team can continue necessary platform work while the PM chooses where product judgment is scarce. Attention allocation is not the same as telling every other function to stop."

Ask

"Which signal feels loudest? Which one is most consequential? Are those the same?"

Take two quick reactions. Do not debate them.

Transition

"The first correction is simple: stop starting from the activity and work backward from the choice."

Slide 4 - Decision-first changes the sequence

Time: 3 minutes Job: Clarify that decision-first changes the sequence of work rather than replacing activity with a premature answer.

Rehearse

Point to the two sequences first:

"The Reforge distinction is decision-last versus decision-first - not activity versus decision. In a decision-last sequence, the team begins with desired data, a broad research question, or a convenient method. It runs the work, produces evidence, and only then asks what decision the findings should change."S1-SN-04
"Decision-first does not mean making the answer before doing the work. Reforge separates two moments: define the decision to be made at the beginning, then make the decision at the end. Between those moments, the team maps the evidence it needs, chooses and executes the research activity, and synthesizes what it learned. The activity remains essential; the decision gives it a job."S1-SN-04
"So the practical correction is about sequence. We move from 'run onboarding discovery and see what emerges' to 'define which roadmap response we need to choose, identify what could discriminate among the options, and then select the activity capable of producing that evidence.'"

Misconception recovery

If someone says a decision can only be made after research:

"Yes - and that is exactly why Reforge uses 'define the decision' at the start and 'make the decision' at the end. Defining the decision establishes the choice the research must inform. It does not preselect the answer."

Transition

"Now let us apply that sequence by defining the actual roadmap decision before we select any evidence activity."

Slide 5 - Roadmap decision boundary

Time: 4 minutes Job: Turn competing roadmap signals into a bounded choice set without selecting the answer prematurely.

Rehearse

"A roadmap conversation rarely begins with one initiative in isolation. It begins with several plausible responses competing for the same attention and capacity. If the alternatives are invisible, the meeting can look like prioritization while quietly assuming the answer."

Walk the boundary before discussing any option:

"The owner is the Noted PM. The horizon is the next two weeks. Capacity permits one primary focus. The choice will be reviewed at the next planning cycle. These constraints make the options comparable without pretending their consequences are identical."

Then point across A through E and be precise that no option has been selected:

"Option A investigates activation before changing onboarding. B earns the enterprise meeting-summary problem before choosing a solution. C prioritizes latency diagnosis. D begins migration scoping. E keeps the current roadmap and waits for exposure or evidence to change. The defer option matters because a list with no legitimate 'not now' is a forced ranking, not a decision."

Close on the implication strip:

"We have framed the decision; we have not made it. Evidence work may support one option, rule one out, or reveal that the set itself is wrong. Once the team selects an option, the remaining alternatives become explicit non-choices: what remains out, for how long, and when it will be reconsidered."

Misconception recovery

If someone says listing options will bias the investigation:

"It can, if the option set is a disguised feature shortlist. A real boundary includes materially different responses, a no-new-commitment option, and permission for evidence to reframe the set. Decision-first narrows the job of evidence; it does not preselect the answer."

Transition

"Once the choice is visible, the next question is not 'How much research is best?' It is 'How much rigor is responsible for this decision?'"

Slide 6 - Five conditions for proportionate rigor

Time: 5 minutes Job: Teach a judgment conversation without creating a score.

Rehearse

"Reforge's decision-architecture material makes impact and reversibility central to decision attention. We keep those principles and extend the judgment with uncertainty, timing, and specialist dependence. None of the five calculates the answer."S1-SN-03

Work row by row:

"Consequence asks what value, harm, trust, cost, or strategic option is exposed. Stakeholder visibility is not consequence."
"Reversibility asks whether the choice can be undone cleanly and who absorbs the reversal cost."
"Uncertainty asks which unknown could realistically reverse the choice. Not every unknown deserves equal attention."
"Timing asks about both errors: waiting too long and moving too soon. Delay can be consequential."
"Expertise asks whose judgment or authority is required. A PM does not become qualified to accept security, legal, statistical, or architecture risk by completing a template."

Then make the anti-score point explicit:

"If you turn this into five numbers and add them, you have replaced a difficult conversation with arithmetic theater. The value of the screen is that it exposes why two responsible people might choose different rigor."

The riskiest consequential hypothesis should receive attention first, but prioritization remains accountable judgment rather than a deterministic matrix.S1-SN-07

Ask

"Which condition is most often missing from prioritization conversations in your company?"

Take two answers, then move on.

Transition

"One of these conditions is more designable than it first appears: reversibility."

Slide 7 - Reversibility is designed

Time: 3 minutes Job: Prevent "experiment" from becoming a magic word.

Rehearse

"Calling something a test does not make it reversible. The operating design does."

Point to the left:

"Replace onboarding for every new workspace is a broad commitment."

Move across the controls:

"Limit exposure to new solo users. Keep a rollback path. Predeclare a stop condition. Bound what happens to free text. Now we have changed the cost of being wrong."

Point to the bounded move:

"A 14-day first-session pilot is not automatically correct, harmless, or evidentially sufficient. It is simply more reviewable and recoverable than the unbounded choice."

Misconception recovery

If someone says, "We can always roll back code":

"Code can roll back while user trust, leaked data, changed behavior, support load, or contractual consequence remains. Technical rollback is one part of product reversibility."

Transition

"You now have enough to make the first call. Do not wait for more case data. The constraint is the point."

Slide 8 - Unit 1 decision

Time: 6 minutes individual work plus 8 minutes debrief Job: Produce one bounded decision and a deliberate exclusion.

Give the instruction

"Choose one decision, not one signal. Write the owner, population, horizon, consequence, reversibility, first uncertainty, and minimum responsible rigor. Then name one activity you will deliberately defer. You have six minutes. Keep your answer private until time ends."

At minute four, prompt:

"If you have written 'investigate,' say what action the investigation could change. If you have written 'improve,' name the actual choice."

Debrief sequence

Ask two learners for answers. Capture only four things: decision, reason against, boundary, revision trigger.

Use this model only after learner answers:

"One defensible shared-case branch is: The Noted PM should decide whether the enterprise request points to a consequential decision-handoff problem worth primary product attention before the next roadmap commitment. This is not yet a decision to build automated summaries. The PM owns the product call; the current population is enterprise team leads in recurring decision-heavy meetings. The first uncertainty is whether loss of meeting meaning creates repeated material rework or missed commitments rather than merely stated interest. The minimum responsible rigor is enough to establish the audience, mechanism, and consequence before product commitment."
"The strongest reasons against this branch are the activation decline and the platform end-of-support deadline. Preserve both in the decision record. Clarify whether the platform work is a separately owned migration, and keep activation diagnosis visible rather than implying that the enterprise branch made those signals disappear."
"A deliberate exclusion could be: do not begin a broad onboarding redesign this week, and do not translate the enterprise request directly into a summary build. The shared-case work is a bounded problem investigation, not permission to commit the roadmap."

Compare reasoning, not conclusions

A reliability or platform decision can also be defensible if the learner makes the product consequence and ownership clear. Challenge answers when:

  • the learner merely selects the reddest metric;
  • the owner or population is missing;
  • "high impact" is asserted without naming the exposed value or harm;
  • reversibility is claimed without controls;
  • the learner tries to investigate all four signals;
  • the deferred item is obviously irrelevant rather than a real trade-off.

Transition

"Your choice may differ from this branch. For a common evidence chain, the shared Noted case will carry the enterprise handoff decision forward. Now we have to form a product view relevant to that choice before certainty is available."

Slide 9 - Three inputs with different jobs

Time: 5 minutes Job: Prevent evidence hierarchy and evidence averaging.

Rehearse

"A product view is not a summary of everything we know. It is the PM's current, accountable synthesis for a decision."
"Quantitative evidence is strongest at pattern, magnitude, population, and time window. It cannot establish the mechanism by itself."
"User context is strongest at circumstance, mechanism, language, constraint, and current alternative. It cannot estimate prevalence by itself."
"Product judgment integrates the inputs with accumulated exposure, priors, trade-offs, and accountability. It cannot create evidence that is missing."

Reforge frames strong decisions as drawing on product data, user insights, and product intuition. The course preserves the distinct contribution of each input but rejects equal boxes, forced agreement, or arithmetic weighting.S1-SN-09

Accumulated feedback exposure can inform judgment, but exposure produces a prior rather than proof.S1-SN-08

Emphasize

"Different jobs means contradiction is not automatically failure. It may be the clue."

Transition

"Look at what happens when the signals disagree across different populations and stages."

Slide 10 - Contradiction can reveal the boundary

Time: 5 minutes Job: Turn conflict into a segmentation and mechanism question.

Rehearse

"This chart is illustrative and not to scale. Do not read the lines as measured series. Read the pattern. New-user activation can decline while retained-team activity rises and recent interview sentiment remains positive. Those observations do not have to cancel one another."
"The first hypothesis should not be 'the evidence is mixed.' That is a description of our discomfort. A stronger hypothesis is that the population or mechanism differs: perhaps new solo users are struggling in the first session while retained teams continue receiving value."
"The wrong move is to average the signals into a neutral story. The right move is to ask which population and mechanism make all three observations possible."

A driver-oriented dashboard can connect outcomes with plausible levers, but the relationship remains a model to challenge rather than causal proof.S1-SN-13

Ask

"What population boundary would you inspect first, and what would make that boundary wrong?"

Take one answer.

Transition

"To make that reasoning challengeable, we need to stop blending the source with our interpretation."

Slide 11 - Reasoning ledger

Time: 4 minutes Job: Make product judgment inspectable without turning it into a bureaucratic log.

Rehearse

"Observation: activation declined 11 percent across six weeks. That statement still needs a metric definition and population boundary, but it reports what the case contains."
"Interpretation: first-session friction may be creating the decline. The word 'may' matters; this is our explanation, not the measurement."
"Prior: past onboarding changes affected solo users more than teams. That experience can guide attention, but we must ask whether the context is still comparable."
"Decision implication: investigate enterprise team handoff before committing to automated summaries, while keeping activation diagnosis separately owned. That connects the current view to the shared decision without pretending the other signal disappeared."

Durable retrieval and categorization make later review possible; a transient stream or vivid recent memory should not become the full evidence base.S1-SN-11 Do not make a causal claim about cognitive bias here; simply ask whether the record overweights what is recent, loud, or easy to recall.S1-SN-12

Ask

"Which line on this slide is easiest for a stakeholder to repeat later as if it were an observation?"

Expected answer: the interpretation.

Transition

"A traceable view is necessary, but it still needs a strength and a condition for revision."

Slide 12 - Confidence with a boundary

Time: 4 minutes Job: Teach position without certainty performance.

Rehearse

"A useful confidence statement has three parts: the current belief, a serious counter-signal, and a revision trigger."
"The current belief is not 'enterprise users need summaries.' It is narrower: retained-team workflow value makes enterprise decision handoff worth investigating, while the mechanism and consequence remain unearned."
"The counter-signal is not a ceremonial caveat. The activation decline may deserve the primary product response instead. That keeps the competing roadmap consequence visible."
"The revision trigger is observable: if the enterprise requests do not connect to repeated material follow-through failure, the handoff branch loses force even if stakeholders still like summaries."

Reforge's communication material supports matching confidence, uncertainty, audience, and requested decision. The course adds an explicit rule: persuasion cannot hide evidence limits or contradiction.S1-SN-14

Misconception recovery

If someone asks for a percentage confidence:

"Use a percentage only if you have a defensible probability model and shared interpretation. In ordinary product work, a precise number often hides the boundary rather than clarifying it. State the conditions under which the view holds and changes."

Transition

"Now you will form the view. The answer must take a position and make it easy to revise."

Slide 13 - Unit 2 decision

Time: 6 minutes individual work plus 8 minutes debrief Job: Produce a current view with lineage, counterevidence, and revision conditions.

Give the instruction

"Write four lines: observation, interpretation, prior, and decision implication. Then add one counter-signal, your confidence boundary, and a credible revision trigger. Six minutes."

At minute four:

"Check whether your observation contains a causal verb. Check whether your interpretation is pretending to describe the entire user base."

Model debrief

After two learner responses, rehearse this answer:

"Observation: the activation index fell from 100 to 89 across six weeks; retained-team activity rises in the illustrative case; recent interviews are positive."
"Interpretation: Noted may have a split product picture. New-user activation risk may be concentrated among solo users, while retained-team activity and positive interviews suggest stronger collaborative workflow value. The enterprise requests may fit that strength, but they do not yet establish the handoff mechanism or consequence."
"Prior: prior onboarding changes affected solo users more than teams, although we have not established that the context is comparable."
"Decision implication: investigate whether enterprise team leads experience repeated material handoff failure before committing to automated summaries. Keep the activation issue separately owned and visible rather than folding it into the enterprise claim."
"Counter-signal: the activation decline may deserve the primary product response, and the enterprise requests may reflect feature preference rather than material follow-through failure. Confidence: bounded, because retained-team value is visible but the handoff mechanism is not established. Revision trigger: targeted evidence fails to connect the request to repeated material consequence for the bounded enterprise audience."

Challenge weak answers

  • "Activation is down because onboarding is bad" combines observation and mechanism.
  • "The interviews are positive, so the metric must be wrong" treats narrow context as a veto.
  • "We need more data" avoids a current position.
  • "High confidence" without population, limitation, or revision trigger performs certainty.
  • "Low confidence" without a decision implication performs caution but provides no judgment.

Decision quality should be reviewed from what was reasonably knowable and how the uncertainty was handled at the time. Later outcomes update the view; they do not retroactively prove that the original reasoning was good or bad.S1-SN-10

Transition to break

"We have a bounded decision and a current view. After the break, we will confront the most common shortcut in product work: treating the requested feature as the problem."

Break - eight minutes

Restart exactly on time. Keep slide 13 visible during the break, then advance to slide 14 when you begin.

Slide 14 - The request compresses six claims

Time: 5 minutes Job: Separate evidence of interest from a problem and value claim.

Rehearse

"Enterprise users ask for automated meeting summaries. The request is real evidence of something: attention, interest, a workflow, perhaps frustration. It is not yet a complete problem definition."
"Inside the request are claims that can fail independently. Which enterprise users? What are they trying to accomplish? Why is meaning lost today? What consequence follows? What workaround exists? Why would they change?"
"If we preserve the request and separate these claims, we do not become anti-solution. We become able to compare the requested solution with alternatives against the same objective."

Reforge's problem, audience, and value material treats these as linked but distinct hypotheses. The course uses them as a revisable system rather than reproducing a PMF narrative template.S1-SN-17S1-SN-18S1-SN-19

Before major commitment, user, problem, and solution/value assumptions should remain visible. The course translates certainty-oriented conviction language into calibrated decision confidence.S1-SN-20

Ask

"If automated summaries disappeared as an option, what objective might remain?"

Possible answers: preserve decisions, clarify owners, reduce rework, or make meeting meaning retrievable. Do not choose one yet.

Transition

"Now we pressure-test whether any of those possible objectives has enough problem evidence behind it."

Slide 15 - Earn the problem definition

Time: 7 minutes Job: Teach "earned" as proportionate, not proven.

Rehearse

"Earned does not mean validated forever. It means the strength and specificity of the claim are proportionate to the evidence, and the unknowns remain visible."

Work the table:

"Presence is partial: three requests and two constructed interviews say the issue occurs somewhere."
"Severity is weak: we have not established a meaningful consequence such as missed commitments, rework, delay, trust loss, or cost."
"Frequency is weak: we do not know which meeting types or how often."
"Ownership is partial: team leads report follow-up burden, but we do not know who experiences or owns the consequence."
"The workaround is visible: manual notes and action-item recaps. A visible workaround matters because value must beat something users already do."
"Commitment is weak: stated interest is not behavior, switching cost, willingness to pay, or another meaningful cost incurred."

Problem presence, severity, frequency, ownership, and workaround are separate claims.S1-SN-17 The informative audience may be narrow, and problem presence does not establish urgency or willingness to change.S1-SN-21 Stated interest, observed behavior, and willingness to incur cost have different evidential strength, but no single behavior proves durable value in every context.S1-SN-22

Concrete past behavior, context, trade-offs, and examples are more informative than feature voting, while detailed interview design belongs in Session 2.S1-SN-23

Misconception recovery

If someone says three customers are enough because enterprise revenue is high:

"They may be enough to justify attention or a bounded service response. They are not automatically enough to claim the mechanism, frequency, or value across enterprise users. Consequence can raise the rigor; it does not repair an evidence boundary."

Transition

"Because the problem is only partially earned, the product feature must remain one option rather than the destination."

Slide 16 - Preserve the alternative set

Time: 6 minutes Job: Keep no-build, workflow, service, product, and deferral options comparable.

Rehearse

"The objective is not to automate summaries. The objective might be to preserve meeting meaning, decisions, and ownership. Once that objective is visible, the option set expands."

Walk across the rows:

  • A decision-log ritual is fast, reversible, and low product commitment.
  • An owner-and-outcome policy changes the workflow rather than the product.
  • Concierge summaries let the team learn with high operating cost and limited product commitment.
  • Automated summaries require more time and product commitment.
  • Deferral is a real option when the problem or strategic consequence has not earned attention.
"These labels are directional comparisons, not scores. The team still has to judge quality, feasibility, trust, privacy, and strategic fit."

Teams should define the change sought before ranking initiatives.S1-SN-15 A stated value proposition remains hypothetical until behavior supports it, and the current alternative determines what improvement the product must earn.S1-SN-19

Ask

"Which option teaches us most about the weakest consequential claim without creating a new high-cost commitment?"

Do not let the room jump directly to concierge as a universal answer. Its operating cost, data handling, and fidelity may make it inappropriate. The question is what it can teach for this claim.

Transition

"Make the call. The acceptable dispositions include proceed, investigate, narrow, reframe, defer, and stop. 'Validated' is not available."

Slide 17 - Unit 3 decision

Time: 6 minutes individual work plus 8 minutes debrief Job: Produce an earned-but-revisable problem hypothesis and a current disposition.

Give the instruction

"Separate the feature request from the objective. Bound the audience, mechanism, severity, frequency, workaround, promised value, and weakest assumption. Choose one disposition and one no-build alternative. Six minutes."

At minute four:

"If your audience is 'enterprise users,' narrow it. If your problem is 'they need summaries,' remove the feature and state the consequence."

Model debrief

After two learner responses:

"A defensible current audience is enterprise team leads who own follow-through after recurring decision-heavy meetings. That is still a hypothesis; the available evidence does not support every enterprise user."
"A defensible objective is to preserve decisions, owners, and context after the meeting. The observed symptom is manual recap burden and occasional loss of meaning. The mechanism remains unproven: it could be poor capture, unclear ownership during the meeting, fragmented retrieval, or weak follow-through rather than absence of a summary."
"Presence is partial. Severity and frequency are weak. The current alternative is manual notes and action-item recap. The promised value is faster shared understanding and fewer missed ownership handoffs relative to that workaround. Commitment evidence is absent."
"The current disposition is investigate, not build. A no-build alternative is an owner-and-outcome meeting ritual or decision-log workflow. The weakest consequential claim is not whether people like summaries. It is whether loss of meeting meaning creates material and repeated rework or missed commitments for this audience."
"That claim becomes the handoff to Session 2. We will choose evidence capable of changing the decision, not collect general opinions about summaries."

Challenge weak answers

  • "Users need automated summaries" preserves the requested solution as the problem.
  • "Enterprise users" is too broad to establish audience validity.
  • "People waste time" needs a mechanism, condition, and consequence.
  • "They said they would use it" is interest, not commitment.
  • "Build an MVP" is a solution commitment, not a disposition justified by the current evidence.
  • "Do nothing" can be valid only when the learner states the consequence of waiting and the trigger for reconsideration.

The weakest consequential link should determine the next evidence priority.S1-SN-24

Transition

"We can now assemble the chain. The point is not the fields. The point is that every later claim can be traced back to the decision and its evidence boundary."

Slide 18 - The Week 1 Product Decision Case

Time: 7 minutes Job: Convert the session into one inspectable learner deliverable.

Rehearse

"Your Week 1 artifact is one linked record. The decision boundary explains why this judgment deserves attention. The current view shows what supports the position and what could reverse it. The linked hypothesis keeps audience, problem, value, and alternative separate. The disposition says what happens next."
"Do not attach three polished templates. If the fields disagree, expose the disagreement. If evidence is missing, narrow the claim. If your real product does not give you responsible access to the evidence, use the Noted route rather than manufacture support."
"The review standard is ex ante reasoning quality: what was knowable, what you treated as observation, which judgment you made, which uncertainty mattered, and what would change your mind. Outcome quality matters later, but it is not allowed to rewrite history."S1-SN-10

Explain the after-session work

Learners spend approximately 75 minutes transferring the record to their real product or continuing with Noted, followed by a 15-minute check-in with the course owner.

In the check-in, ask only:

  1. What is the decision?
  2. What is the strongest evidence against your current view?
  3. Which claim is consequential enough to drive Session 2 evidence work?

Do not edit the learner's prose live. Diagnose the reasoning.

Transition

"The record is useful only if it points forward. The next move is chosen by the weakest consequential claim."

Slide 19 - Handoff to Session 2

Time: 4 minutes plus 10 minutes open Q&A Job: Close the loop and protect the scope of Session 2.

Rehearse

"Session 1 ends with a bounded decision and a current hypothesis. Session 2 will not ask, 'What research method should we run?' It will ask, 'Which evidence could change this decision, and what can that evidence actually justify?'"
"The weakest claim is not automatically the least supported claim. It is the unsupported claim whose failure would most change the decision. That is why consequence and uncertainty stay linked."
"Before Session 2, apply the Week 1 record to your own product, or continue with Noted. Bring the claim you most need to challenge, not a list of everything you would like to know."

Final check

Ask learners to complete this sentence aloud or in chat:

"The decision I am carrying forward is ____. The claim most capable of changing it is ____."

Open Q&A boundary

Use the final ten minutes for conceptual questions. If a question becomes a private product consultation, answer the principle and move the specific case to the learner's 15-minute check-in.

Close with:

"A PM earns trust by making the chain of judgment visible: what we chose, what we knew, what we inferred, what remained uncertain, and what we will do when the world disagrees."

Facilitation diagnostics

If the room is too quiet

  • Ask for a one-sentence decision, not a volunteer to explain everything.
  • Offer two deliberately flawed answers and ask which failure is more dangerous.
  • Use the chat for simultaneous submission, then select two contrasting responses yourself.
  • Do not fill the silence with more teaching before the six-minute timer ends.

If the room becomes framework-hungry

Say:

"The structures on the slides are diagnostic prompts, not a certification checklist. The test is whether your reasoning travels to a different product situation."

Then return to one case choice.

If learners want the canonical Noted answer

Say:

"There are stronger and weaker answers, but not one priority that falls out of the slide. A reliability or platform decision can beat the activation decision if the consequence, ownership, and timing are made explicit. I am testing whether your decision is inspectable and proportionate."

If learners conflate 'core PM' with anti-building

Say:

"Building remains one way to learn or create value. This course refuses to make it the default proof of PM competence. The product option must earn its place against workflow, service, policy, and no-build alternatives."

If learners treat AI as the answer to evidence scarcity

Say:

"AI can retrieve, cluster, compare, and challenge available inputs. It cannot make the wrong population relevant, turn constructed evidence into market proof, or accept the consequence of the decision. Lower analysis cost increases the need to choose the right question."

If time is running short

Protect, in order:

  1. all three six-minute decisions;
  2. the Unit 3 debrief;
  3. the Week 1 handoff;
  4. direct Q&A.

Compress examples on slides 6, 10, and 16. Do not remove the learner decisions or silently skip the provenance distinction.
